label: D5
title: Average and spread, and why the average is not the person

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
This section turns a distribution into two single numbers: a typical value, and how spread out the rest are around it.

The mean of a set of values is their sum divided by how many there are. The median is the middle value of the same set once it is ordered from smallest to largest; where the count is even, it is the mean of the two middle values.

The first quartile is the median of the lower half of the ordered values, and the third quartile is the median of the upper half. The second quartile is the median of the whole set. When the count itself is odd, leave the middle value out of both halves before taking their medians. The interquartile range is the third quartile minus the first, and it describes the spread of the middle half of the values, ignoring anything beyond it.

The population is the whole group a question is about. The sample is the part of that group that was actually measured.

The deviation of a value from the mean is that value minus the mean. The variance is worked out from the squared deviations: add them, then divide by the count for a whole population, or by one less than the count for a sample. The standard deviation is the square root of the variance, expressed in the same unit as the original values, because taking a square root undoes the squaring. To say how far one value sits from the mean in standard deviations, divide its deviation by the standard deviation.

The mean of a set of values says nothing on its own about where any one member of the set actually sits.

blocks.label: In plain terms
blocks.html:
Take six numbers: 5, 8, 12, 15, 20, 40. Add them and divide by how many there are. That is the mean, which everyday speech calls the average.

5 plus 8 plus 12 plus 15 plus 20 plus 40 = 100
100 divided by 6 = 16.6666666667…

The mean is about 16.7.

For the median, put the same six numbers in order, which they already are, and find the middle. With six values there is no single middle one, so take the two in the middle and average them.

12 plus 15 = 27
27 divided by 2 = 13.5

The median is 13.5, noticeably below the mean of 16.7. One number in this set, the 40, sits a long way above the rest. It drags the mean up with it and leaves the median almost where it would have been without it.

Take eight ordered numbers: 2, 4, 4, 6, 8, 8, 10, 12. The middle value, the second quartile, is the average of the two central values.

6 plus 8 = 14
14 divided by 2 = 7

Now split the set into its lower half and its upper half, four numbers each, and find the middle of each half the same way. The lower half is 2, 4, 4, 6.

4 plus 4 = 8
8 divided by 2 = 4

That gives the first quartile, 4. Now the upper half, 8, 8, 10, 12.

8 plus 10 = 18
18 divided by 2 = 9

That gives the third quartile, 9. The interquartile range is the third quartile minus the first.

9 minus 4 = 5

It says the middle half of these eight values is spread across five units.

Now the standard deviation, step by step, on six more bare numbers: 5, 7, 3, 7, 10, 4.

First, the mean.

5 plus 7 plus 3 plus 7 plus 10 plus 4 = 36
36 divided by 6 = 6

The mean is 6. Now the deviation of every value: how far it sits from that mean, kept with its sign.

5 minus 6 = -1
7 minus 6 = 1
3 minus 6 = -3
7 minus 6 = 1
10 minus 6 = 4
4 minus 6 = -2

Square every deviation next, which means multiplying each one by itself. A negative number times a negative number gives a positive number.

-1 times -1 = 1
1 times 1 = 1
-3 times -3 = 9
1 times 1 = 1
4 times 4 = 16
-2 times -2 = 4

Add the squares.

1 plus 1 = 2
2 plus 9 = 11
11 plus 1 = 12
12 plus 16 = 28
28 plus 4 = 32

Divide that by one less than the count of values, which is five here, not six. That division is the variance.

32 divided by 5 = 6.4

The variance is 6.4, and it is in the wrong unit. Squaring every deviation squared the unit too, so a variance worked out from kilograms is really in kilograms squared, which nobody can picture. Take the square root and the unit comes back to the one you started in. That last step is the standard deviation.

square root of 6.4 = 2.529822128

The standard deviation of these six numbers is about 2.53.

Go back to the division by five rather than six. Most papers do the same thing: a sample’s variance is divided by one less than the count. Distances from the sample’s own mean come out a little small on average, because that mean sits in the middle of these particular numbers. Dividing by one less than the count makes the variance come out right on average. The textbook this book follows puts it briefly: dividing by one less ‘gives a better estimate of the population variance’.

blocks.alt: Six dots on a number line at 5, 8, 12, 15, 20 and 40. A solid line marks the median at 13.5, between 12 and 15. A dashed line marks the mean at 16.7, to the right of 15, pulled towards the lone dot at 40.
blocks.caption: The six numbers from this section on one line. The median, 13.5, sits in the middle of the crowd. The mean, 16.7, has been pulled towards the single value of 40. Without it, both would be 12.

blocks.label: Illustration
blocks.html:
Open Table 1 of the paper used in the section on variation: Kiran, Harshitha and Bhargava, 282 medical students in Mangaluru. It gives weight, height, body-mass index and more, each as a mean with its standard deviation beside a median with its first and third quartiles. Papers write the standard deviation (SD) by its two initials. Read the first two rows for the 131 men.

indicator mean (SD) median (first and third quartiles)
weight (kg) 72.0 (13.1) 70.9 (167.7, 177.8)
height (cm) 172.2 (6.8) 173 (62.6, 80.9)

Stop on the weight row’s two quartiles, and check them yourself. The median has to sit between the two quartiles printed beside it: the first quartile below it, the third above it. Here the median is 70.9, and the two numbers printed beside it are 167.7 and 177.8. 70.9 sits below both of them, not between them.

Try the same check on the height row underneath it. The median there is 173, and the two numbers printed beside it are 62.6 and 80.9. It sits above both of them, not between them either.

Both rows fail, in opposite directions. Each passes against the other row’s numbers: 70.9 sits between 62.6 and 80.9, and 173 between 167.7 and 177.8. The numbers fit if the two rows’ quartiles were printed in each other’s places.

Men’s mean body-mass index is 24.2 kilograms per square metre, with a standard deviation of 3.9.

Forty-two of the men are in the band from 25 to 29.9. Ten more are at 30 or more.

42 plus 10 = 52

Fifty-two of the 131 men have a body-mass index of 25 or more.

52 divided by 131 = 0.396946565…
0.396946565 times 100 = 39.6946565

That rounds to about 39.7 per cent, close to two in every five. The mean of the group, 24.2, sits under the line at 25. Close to two in five of the individual men in that same group sit at it or above it. The mean describes the group. It was never a description of any one of the 131 men. Deciding whether one particular man is above or below 25 needs his own reading, not the group’s average.

Men’s mean body fat is 22.1 per cent and their median is 20.3 per cent. The mean sits above the median.

22.1 minus 20.3 = 1.8

By the median’s own definition, at least half of the 131 men have a body fat percentage at or below 20.3. That is also below the mean of 22.1. The men above the median must reach far enough up to pull the mean past it. The quartiles printed beside the median show it: 16.7 and 28.8.

20.3 minus 16.7 = 3.6
28.8 minus 20.3 = 8.5

The first quartile sits 3.6 below the median, and the third sits 8.5 above it. The quarter of men just above the median stretches more than twice as far as the quarter just below it. That is a longer stretch running upward than downward. It is exactly the shape the section on variation described in words.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html:
Checking a median against its own two quartiles catches a pair of quartiles that sits nowhere near the median.

The mean sitting below 25 while many men sit above it is a fact about this one group. It is 131 men, measured this way, in this college, in 2019. It says nothing about any other group. It says nothing about any one of these men beyond what his own reading gives you.

The standard deviation and the interquartile range answer different questions about the same spread. Neither can be worked out from the other.

points.html: A long tail on one side of a distribution pulls the mean toward it. Reading this backwards, “the mean is higher, so most values are higher”, is an error.

Compute the median alongside the mean whenever a handful of extreme values might be present. Compare the two before you quote either one on its own. A gap between them is itself a finding, not a rounding difference to ignore.
A mean, on its own, says nothing about any one person in the group it was computed from.
Divide by one less than the count whenever you compute a standard deviation from a sample.
A mean sitting below a cut-off does not mean most of a group is below it.
Check a printed median against the two quartiles printed beside it before you trust any of the three.

In a lopsided distribution, the standard deviation hides that the two sides spread out differently. Where the mean and median disagree by much, look at the quartiles instead of trusting a single standard deviation to describe both sides.

blocks.prompt:
A report states this. “Average daily step count in our clinic’s patients is 6,200, comfortably above the report’s own target of 5,000 steps. So inactivity is not a major concern here.” (The figures are made up for this exercise.)

The same report’s raw data shows a median of 4,100 steps. Say what the gap between the two numbers tells you. Say what you would ask for before agreeing with the conclusion.
blocks.answer:
The mean, 6,200, sits well above the median, 4,100. The patients above the median reach far enough up to pull the mean past it. At least half of all patients walk at or below 4,100 steps, which is already under the report’s own target of 5,000.

“Comfortably above the target” describes the mean, not the typical patient. The typical patient, by the median, sits below it.

What to ask for instead: the proportion of patients whose own step count sits below 5,000. Work that out directly, rather than inferring it from the average. That number, not the mean, answers the question the report is actually trying to answer.

blocks.prompt:
A first-year resident reads a paper’s abstract, sees a mean below a clinical cut-off, and concludes “so this group is fine”. You have ten minutes and a whiteboard.

Teach them why a mean sitting below a cut-off does not mean the group is.
blocks.answer:
Ten minutes, for somebody who expects a mechanism.

Write two numbers on the board. One is a mean of 24.2, from a real study of 131 men. The other is 25, the WHO cut-off that paper used. Both are body-mass index, in kilograms per square metre. Ask the resident what the mean means for the group.

They will likely say the group is under the cut-off. Write a second real fact from the same study underneath: 52 of the 131 men individually have a body-mass index of 25 or more.

52 divided by 131 = 0.396946565…
0.396946565 times 100 = 39.6946565

About 39.7 per cent, close to two in five. Let the resident sit with that fact. The mean is under the line. Nearly two in five of the actual men are at it or over.

Ask what would have to be true for the mean to sit below 25 while some men sit above it. The answer is that other men sit far enough below 25 to balance them out. Nothing about the mean tells you how many are on which side, or by how much.

Close with the rule to carry into the next chart they read. A mean below a line is a fact about the mean. Whether most of the group is below that same line is a different question. Whether the one patient in front of them is below it is a third. Both need the group’s spread, not just its average.

blocks.prompt:
Find the mean and the median of these seven numbers.

4    9    2    15    7    9    3
blocks.answer:
The mean first.

4 plus 9 plus 2 plus 15 plus 7 plus 9 plus 3 = 49
49 divided by 7 = 7

For the median, order the numbers first.

2    3    4    7    9    9    15

Seven numbers, so the middle one is the fourth. That is 7.

The mean and the median both come out at 7 here. They do not have to agree, and the next problem shows a case where they do not.

blocks.prompt:
Find the mean and the median of these six numbers.

6    9    11    14    18    50
blocks.answer:
The mean.

6 plus 9 plus 11 plus 14 plus 18 plus 50 = 108
108 divided by 6 = 18

The median. The numbers are already ordered. With six of them, average the two in the middle.

11 plus 14 = 25
25 divided by 2 = 12.5

12.5.

The mean, 18, sits well above the median, 12.5. The single value 50 is pulling the mean upward while the median stays close to where five of the six values actually are.

blocks.prompt:
These eight numbers are already ordered.

3    5    5    9    11    11    15    19

Find the first quartile, the second quartile, the third quartile, and the interquartile range.
blocks.answer:
The second quartile is the median of the whole set. With eight numbers, average the two in the middle.

9 plus 11 = 20
20 divided by 2 = 10

The second quartile is 10.

The lower half is 3, 5, 5, 9. Its middle two are the second and third values.

5 plus 5 = 10
10 divided by 2 = 5

The first quartile is 5.

The upper half is 11, 11, 15, 19.

11 plus 15 = 26
26 divided by 2 = 13

The third quartile is 13. The interquartile range is the third quartile minus the first.

13 minus 5 = 8

The interquartile range is 8.

blocks.prompt:
These seven numbers are already ordered.

2    5    7    9    12    15    20

Find the first quartile, the second quartile, the third quartile, and the interquartile range.
blocks.answer:
Seven is odd, so the middle value, the fourth one, is the second quartile on its own. Leave it out of both halves before you take their medians.

second quartile = 9

The lower half, with the middle value left out, is 2, 5, 7. Its own middle value is the first quartile.

first quartile = 5

The upper half, with the middle value left out, is 12, 15, 20. Its own middle value is the third quartile.

third quartile = 15

The interquartile range is the third quartile minus the first.

15 minus 5 = 10

The interquartile range is 10. Software sometimes computes quartiles by a different rule and can print a slightly different number from this one. That is not a sign either calculation is wrong.

blocks.prompt:
Work out the sample standard deviation of these six numbers, step by step.

8    6    10    4    12    8
blocks.answer:
The mean first.

8 plus 6 plus 10 plus 4 plus 12 plus 8 = 48
48 divided by 6 = 8

The deviation of every value from the mean.

8 minus 8 = 0
6 minus 8 = -2
10 minus 8 = 2
4 minus 8 = -4
12 minus 8 = 4
8 minus 8 = 0

Square every deviation.

0 times 0 = 0
-2 times -2 = 4
2 times 2 = 4
-4 times -4 = 16
4 times 4 = 16
0 times 0 = 0

Add the squares.

0 plus 4 = 4
4 plus 4 = 8
8 plus 16 = 24
24 plus 16 = 40
40 plus 0 = 40

Divide by one less than the count, which is five.

40 divided by 5 = 8

The variance is 8. Take its square root for the standard deviation.

square root of 8 = 2.828427125

The sample standard deviation is about 2.83.

blocks.prompt:
Give the sample variance and the sample standard deviation of a sample whose deviations from its own mean are the five values below.

-2    4    -1    3    -4
blocks.answer:
Square each deviation.

-2 times -2 = 4
4 times 4 = 16
-1 times -1 = 1
3 times 3 = 9
-4 times -4 = 16

Add them.

4 plus 16 = 20
20 plus 1 = 21
21 plus 9 = 30
30 plus 16 = 46

Divide by one less than the count, which is four.

46 divided by 4 = 11.5

The variance is 11.5. The standard deviation is its square root.

square root of 11.5 = 3.391164992

The standard deviation is about 3.39.

blocks.prompt:
Table 1 of Kiran et al. (2022) gives men’s mean body-mass index as 24.2 kg/m2 and their median as 23.8 kg/m2.

Work out the gap between the two, and say which side of the distribution its tail is likely on.
blocks.answer:
24.2 minus 23.8 = 0.4

The gap is 0.4 kg/m2.

The mean sits a little above the median. That pattern happens when values above the median pull the mean upward more than values below it pull it down. The gap here is small next to the spread of the whole group. So this is only a slight sign of a tail on the high side, not a firm one.

blocks.prompt:
Men’s body-mass index in the same table has a median of 23.8 kg/m2, with the two quartiles printed beside it as 21.2 and 26.8.

Work out the interquartile range as a single number, and check whether the median sits between the two quartiles it is printed beside.
blocks.answer:
26.8 minus 21.2 = 5.6

The interquartile range is 5.6 kg/m2.

Check the median against the two quartiles. 23.8 sits between 21.2 and 26.8. So this row of the table is internally consistent, unlike the weight row worked through in the illustration above.

blocks.prompt:
The same table prints men’s body-mass index as a median of 23.8 kg/m2, with a first quartile of 21.2 and a third quartile of 26.8.

Work out how far each quartile sits from the median. Say what the two distances suggest about which side of the distribution has the longer tail.
blocks.answer:
23.8 minus 21.2 = 2.6
26.8 minus 23.8 = 3.0

The first quartile sits 2.6 kg/m2 below the median, and the third sits 3.0 above it. So the quarter of men just above the median is spread a little wider than the quarter just below it. That points the same way as the mean sitting above the median in the level 4 problem: a tail on the high side. The two distances differ by only 0.4, so this is a slight sign, not a firm one.

blocks.prompt:
Suppose a man in this group had a body-mass index of 30 kg/m2. The men’s mean is 24.2 with a standard deviation of 3.9.

Work out how many standard deviations above the mean his reading would sit.
blocks.answer:
Find the deviation first.

30 minus 24.2 = 5.8

Divide by the standard deviation to express it in standard deviations.

5.8 divided by 3.9 = 1.487179487

That reading would sit about 1.49 standard deviations above the men’s mean.

blocks.prompt:
Table 1 of Kiran et al. (2022) gives the 151 women’s body fat as a mean of 33.8 per cent. The median is 34.0 per cent, with the two quartiles printed beside it as 28.1 and 39.2.

Work out the interquartile range as a single number. Check whether the median sits between the two quartiles. Then say which way the mean sitting below the median points.
blocks.answer:
39.2 minus 28.1 = 11.1

The interquartile range is 11.1 percentage points.

Check the median against the two quartiles. 34.0 sits between 28.1 and 39.2, so this row is internally consistent.

Here the mean, 33.8, sits below the median, 34.0, the other way round from the men’s rows worked through above. A mean below the median happens when the values below the median reach further down than those above it reach up. If this pattern holds, the tail here points toward the low side rather than the high side.

blocks.prompt:
Five patients were picked from a clinic’s much larger patient list. Here is someone’s worked sample standard deviation of their ages, in years. Find the step that broke.

the numbers are 12, 15, 9, 21, 18
mean = (12 plus 15 plus 9 plus 21 plus 18) divided by 5 = 15
deviations: -3, 0, -6, 6, 3
squares: 9, 0, 36, 36, 9
sum of squares = 90
variance = 90 divided by 5 = 18
standard deviation = square root of 18 = 4.242640687
blocks.answer:
The mean, the deviations and the squares are all correct, and so is their sum, 90. The step that broke is the division for the variance.

These five patients are a sample from the clinic’s larger list, and the question asked for the sample standard deviation. Its variance divides the sum of squared deviations by one less than the count, which is four here, not five.

90 divided by 4 = 22.5

The variance is 22.5, not 18. Take its square root.

square root of 22.5 = 4.743416490

The correct standard deviation is about 4.74, not 4.24.

Why it looks reasonable: dividing by the count of values, five, is exactly what the mean itself does two lines earlier. Re-using the same 5 feels consistent. The sample rule uses one less than the count only at this one step. It appears nowhere else in the working, which is exactly what makes it easy to miss.

blocks.prompt:
A teammate is about to quote this line from Table 1 of Kiran et al. (2022) in a talk.

“Median weight among the women was 57.4 kilograms, with quartiles of 155.0 and 163.0.”

Find what is wrong with the line. Say what you would check before quoting any pair of quartiles taken from a table you have not read closely.
blocks.answer:
The median has to sit between the two quartiles printed beside it. Here the median, 57.4, sits below both 155.0 and 163.0, not between them, so the three numbers cannot all describe the same row.

The height row printed just below it gives a median of 159, with 51.3 and 63.9 printed beside it. Swap the two rows’ quartiles and check both medians again. The weight row’s median, 57.4, sits between the height row’s printed numbers, 51.3 and 63.9. The height row’s median, 159, sits between the weight row’s printed numbers, 155.0 and 163.0. Both checks pass with the quartiles swapped. The numbers fit if the two rows’ quartiles were printed in each other’s places, the same pattern as in the men’s rows above.

What to check before quoting any pair of quartiles: does the paired median actually sit between the two quartiles printed with it. That check takes a moment, and it is the one this line fails.

blocks.prompt:
Somebody makes this claim from the body fat figures in Table 1 of Kiran et al. (2022).

“The mean body fat among the men is 22.1 per cent and the median is 20.3 per cent. Since the mean is higher, most men must have a body fat percentage above 22.1.”

Find the error in the reasoning.
blocks.answer:
The conclusion has the direction backwards. By the median’s own definition, at least half of the men are at or below 20.3. And 20.3 sits below the mean of 22.1. So at least half of the men are below the mean, not above it.

The men above the median reach far enough up to pull the mean past it. At least half sit at or below the median.

Why it looks reasonable: “the mean is higher, so more men must be higher” sounds right. It is the wrong direction. A higher mean is the sign of a tail on the high side. Some readings go far up. It is not a sign that most readings sit above the mean.

blocks.prompt:
A note about the study says this. “Women’s average body-mass index was 23.0, under the cut-off of 25, so weight was not a concern in this group of students.”

Decide what to compute, compute it, and say what your answer does not establish.
blocks.answer:
What to compute: where the women’s own quartiles sit against 25, rather than resting on the group’s average. Table 1 prints the women’s body-mass index as 22.7 (20.5, 25.6). That is a median of 22.7, with quartiles of 20.5 and 25.6.

25.6 minus 25 = 0.6

The third quartile, 25.6, sits 0.6 above the cut-off. About a quarter of the women sit at or above 25.6. Since 25.6 is above 25, at least about a quarter of the 151 women are at 25 or above, even though the mean is 23.0.

What this does not establish. Body-mass index does not measure body fat directly. It cannot tell fat from lean mass. So this figure does not establish anything about any one woman’s health.

Nor does it show that 25 is where risk starts for this group. The figure 25 is the WHO cut-off the paper used. The same paper notes that some Asian groups show metabolic risk at a lower body-mass index than that. And it says nothing about students elsewhere. This figure is for one college in one year.

blocks.prompt:
A colleague says this about the same study. “Body fat in this group of men averages 22 per cent, so most men have a body fat percentage somewhere between 20 and 24.”

Decide what to compute, compute it, and say what your answer does not establish.
blocks.answer:
What to compute: what the quartiles in the same row of Table 1 say about where the men sit. That is better than guessing a narrow band around the mean.

Men’s body fat is printed as a median of 20.3 per cent, with quartiles of 16.7 and 28.8.

28.8 minus 16.7 = 12.1

By definition, about a quarter of the men sit at or below 16.7 and about a quarter sit at or above 28.8. So about half the men lie between 16.7 and 28.8. The colleague’s 20 to 24 sits inside that stretch, so at most about half can lie in it. The mean, 22.1, also sits above the median, 20.3, by 1.8 points.

22.1 minus 20.3 = 1.8

The median says at least half of the men sit at or below 20.3. The men above it reach far enough up to pull the mean past it.

What this does not establish. Neither the mean nor the quartiles tell you what fraction of men actually fall inside 20 to 24 specifically. That needs a frequency table of the individual readings, the way Table 2 gave one for body-mass index. No such table is given here for body fat. And the quartiles already show that “most men” cannot be packed into a band as narrow as 20 to 24.
